631.title: The honey forest
631.hook: the search party wants to storm Lanka itself, an old bear says no, and then they raid the king's honey
631.carry: svadharma: do your own part, offer the rest
631.howItsDone: Many Hindus close a task or a puja with the word Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna, a habit drawn from the Gita's teaching on offering the fruit of action; the Madhuvana raid stays a favorite comic scene in Sundara Kanda recitations.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the return. Arishta sinking, the sky like an ocean, and your line: the Sundara Kanda, the book where hope returns.
screen: `SUNDARA KANDA: THE BOOK WHERE HOPE RETURNS.`

segments.voice: On the way home to Kishkindha, the search party is giddy. Hanuman has found Sita. They've crossed back over the sea. And Prince Angada has a big idea: why go home at all? Why not finish this ourselves? Before the honey and the dancing, an old bear has to stop them from doing a job that isn't theirs.
screen: `THE NEWS, AND A BIG IDEA.` → `WHY NOT FINISH IT OURSELVES?`

segments.voice: Angada's plan sounds brave: go back to Lanka, defeat Ravana, and bring Sita to Rama. Jambavan, the old bear, the eldest of the party, says no. We were sent to find her and to tell Rama. That was our task. The rescue is Rama's, and Sita herself said it in the grove: let Rama come for me. So they turn north. And then, with their own job done, they celebrate. They reach the Madhuvana, King Sugriva's guarded honey forest, and with Angada's permission they fall on it: eating, drinking, dancing, tumbling out of the trees. When the guardian, Dadhimukha, Sugriva's uncle, tries to stop them, they shove him around. He runs to the king, furious. And Sugriva smiles. They'd never dare, he tells Rama, unless they'd succeeded. Sita has been found. Here's the teaching under the comedy. Hindus call it svadharma, your own dharma: the duty that is truly yours, by your place in life and your nature. The Bhagavad Gita says it boldly: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Jambavan knew the monkeys' part was to search and report, and the rescue was Rama's. Many teachers read Hanuman's whole life this way: he does his own part completely, then lays the result at Rama's feet. The Gita calls that karma yoga: do what's yours, and offer the fruit.
screen: `STORM LANKA? JAMBAVAN SAYS NO.` · `THE HONEY FOREST.` · `THEY'D NEVER DARE UNLESS...` · `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DUTY.` · then, large: `DO YOUR PART, OFFER THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and bring to mind one thing that's weighing on you this week. Ask Jambavan's question: which part of this is mine, and which part belongs to someone else? Name your part plainly. Many Hindus finish a task, or a puja, with one word: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. If you pray, say it softly over your part. If you don't, simply breathe out and set the rest down.
The return. Jambavan sends the party home with only its own work done, and Sugriva reads the wrecked honey forest as proof that Sita has been found.
Your line: svadharma, do your own part, offer the rest. Tomorrow, Hanuman stands in front of Rama at last. See you there.

632.title: Seen: Hanuman's first word
632.hook: Hanuman has the biggest news of Rama's life, and he chooses his first word with care
632.carry: vak tapas: speech that's true, kind and calming
632.howItsDone: Ramayana teachers, in temples and in family readings, often pause on Hanuman's first word, seen, as a lesson in the Gita's discipline of speech; Kamban's Tamil Ramayana gives the same moment as I saw.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the return. Jambavan left the rescue to Rama, the monkeys raided the honey forest, and your line was svadharma, do your own part, offer the rest.

Rama has been waiting on a mountain outside Kishkindha. The search parties from the north, the east and the west have already come back with nothing. Now the southern party arrives, loud and happy, and Hanuman steps forward. He has crossed the sea, found her, spoken with her, fought half of Lanka and left it burning. He has a long, astonishing story to tell. And first he has to decide which word comes out of his mouth.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, AND NO NEWS.` → `THREE PARTIES CAME BACK EMPTY.` → `WHICH WORD FIRST?`

segments.voice: The word he puts first, in Valmiki's Sanskrit, is drishta. Seen. He bows and tells Rama the queen has been seen, that she is keeping her vows, that she is unharmed. Think about the order. If he had begun with the ocean, or Lanka, or the words I went, Rama would have spent every sentence waiting, heart in his throat. If he had begun with her name alone, Rama might have braced for the worst. Seen comes first, and the fear is answered before it can rise. The Tamil poet Kamban, retelling the story, makes it even sharper: his Hanuman opens with the Tamil for I saw, before he names her at all. Only then does Hanuman tell the rest: the leap, the city at night, the ashoka grove, a thin woman under a tree, Ravana's threats, Rama's own ring passed down through the branches. Joy comes over Rama and Lakshmana as they listen. Sugriva had already guessed, from the monkeys' wild celebration on the way home. Hindus have a name for this kind of care. The Bhagavad Gita calls it the tapas, the discipline, of speech: words that are true, kind and helpful, and that don't stir up fear. Speech is part of your spiritual practice, not just your manners. And Hanuman is its great example. When Rama first met him in the forest, he told Lakshmana he'd never heard anyone speak so well. Here, with the biggest news of Rama's life, Hanuman proves it: before he speaks, he thinks about where his words will land.

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep mauna, a short stretch of silence, as part of their practice. Sit in mauna now for a few breaths. Then think of one piece of news you'll bring someone soon, and try the Gita's test: is it true, is it kind, does it help, will it ease their fear rather than raise it? Find the first word that answers their fear. If you pray, offer your words before you speak them.

633.title: Sita's jewel
633.hook: a hair jewel, a story only Rama would know, and a month on the clock: the beautiful book comes to rest
633.carry: shravana: hearing the story again is devotion
633.howItsDone: Hindu families and temples recite the Sundara Kanda on its own as a complete reading, often over several days and especially in difficult times, and it closes with Rama holding Sita's jewel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman put seen first, so Rama's fear was answered before the story began. Your line: vak tapas, speech that's true, kind and calming.

Hanuman has told the story. Now he opens his hand. In it is a jewel Sita wore in her hair; in the ashoka grove she untied it and gave it to him, so that Rama would believe every word. Rama takes it, holds it against his chest, and weeps. Lakshmana stands beside him. To anyone else it's an ornament. To the two men looking at it, it's her.
screen: `HANUMAN OPENS HIS HAND.` → `A JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` → `RAMA WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Rama knows the jewel at once. In Valmiki he says it came to Sita from her father, King Janaka, at their wedding, and that seeing it is almost like seeing her. Then he asks Hanuman again and again: what did she say? Tell me her exact words. So Hanuman passes on everything. Sita had sent a second token, and it was a story: the crow at Chitrakuta that kept attacking her, and the single blade of grass Rama sent after it as a weapon. Nobody else was there. A memory used as a password. And she sent a message with a deadline: she could hold on for one more month, and no longer. So the joy of seen arrives with a clock attached, and Rama's grief and resolve rise together. Why is this book called Sundara, beautiful? People give different answers, and nobody can say for certain which one Valmiki meant. But Hindu tradition treats the Sundara Kanda as a book of hope. It's recited on its own, start to finish, at home or in a temple, especially in hard times, because it's the stretch of the story where the lost is found and the long wait finally hears seen. And notice where it comes to rest: on a man asking to hear her words one more time. Devotees do the same with Rama's story. The Bhagavata Purana lists shravana, hearing the Lord's stories, first among the forms of devotion. Families who know every line of the Sundara Kanda still read it whole, again, because hearing it again is the prayer.
screen: `HER FATHER'S JEWEL.` · `A MEMORY AS A PASSWORD.` · `ONE MORE MONTH.` · `THE BOOK OF HOPE.` · then, large: `SHRAVANA: HEARING IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a little shravana every day: a few verses read aloud, a bhajan, a recording of the Sundara Kanda playing while they cook. Try it now. If you pray, softly repeat the old Rama chant, Sri Rama, Jaya Rama, Jaya Jaya Rama, a few times, and simply listen to it. If you don't, bring to mind the words of someone you love, the way Rama asked for Sita's, and hear them once more.
Seen, Sita. The news that closes the Sundara Kanda, carried home with a jewel from her hair, a story only Rama would know, and one month on the clock.
Your line: shravana, hearing the story again is devotion. Tomorrow the war book, the Yuddha Kanda, begins. Until tomorrow.

634.title: An army on the shore
634.hook: the war book opens with an embrace, a march, and God in human form awake by the sea
634.carry: an avatar weeps: God took on a human heart
634.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes and temples keep an image of Rama's court, the Ram darbar, with Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet, and teachers call Rama maryada purushottama: God living a human life within its limits.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's jewel, a crow story only Rama would know, and your line: shravana, hearing the story again is devotion. Today the sixth book begins: the Yuddha Kanda, the war book.

The war book doesn't open with a war. It opens with a thank-you. Rama turns to Hanuman and tries to say what he's done: crossed an ocean, found her, come back. Then Rama looks at himself: an exile in bark clothes, living on a mountain, with no kingdom, no treasury, no land to give. So he says the one gift he has left is this, and he takes Hanuman in his arms.
screen: `NOT A WAR. A THANK-YOU.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO GIVE.` → `AN EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Then the thank-you turns into a question. Hanuman crossed the ocean by leaping. An army can't leap. How will all of us get across? Sugriva answers like a good friend in a crisis: grief makes a person slow; let's march, and find the way when we're there. So the army pours south over hills and forests, Hanuman carrying Rama on his shoulders at times, and makes camp on the last shore of the land. In front of them, the ocean, roaring, with no far shore in sight. That night Rama can't rest. He speaks to the wind: you blow where she is. Touch her, and then come and touch me. Now remember who Rama is, for Hindus. He's an avatar: Vishnu himself, come down to earth. And look at what the avatar does. He grieves. He can't sleep. He doesn't know the way across, and he leans on a friend. That isn't a flaw in the story; it's the teaching. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of men, living within limits. In this avatar, God doesn't skip the human part. He keeps his word, he loves, he weeps, he asks for help. Many teachers say that's why people love Rama so much: he knows a long night by the water from the inside.
screen: `HOW WILL WE ALL GET ACROSS?` · `THE ARMY MARCHES SOUTH.` · `RAMA SPEAKS TO THE WIND.` · `AN AVATAR WHO GRIEVES.` · then, large: `GOD TOOK ON A HUMAN HEART.`

635.title: The ocean rises
635.hook: three nights of asking, one burst of anger, and the ocean rises as a god with a nature of his own
635.carry: the elements are sacred, each with its nature
635.howItsDone: Many Hindus say a morning prayer to the earth, Bhudevi, asking pardon for the touch of their feet before they step out of bed; at Rameswaram, the coastal town tradition links with this shore, pilgrims bathe in the sea.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, before a single stone. Rama awake on the shore at night, asking the wind to touch her, and your line, an avatar weeps, God took on a human heart.

Rama spreads kusha grass on the sand, the sharp ritual grass, and lies down on it, facing the sea. He folds his hands, asking the god of the ocean, Sagara, to show him a way across. One night passes. Nothing. Two nights. Three nights, fasting, waiting, and the water just keeps coming in and going out as if no one were there.
screen: `A BED OF KUSHA GRASS.` → `THREE NIGHTS OF ASKING.` → `NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On the fourth morning Rama gets up angry. Gentleness, he tells Lakshmana, is taken for weakness. He takes up his bow and fires into the sea. The waves heave, the sea creatures thrash, the water churns as if the end of the world had come. Lakshmana catches his brother's arm: enough. And Rama fits a terrible weapon to the bow, ready to dry the ocean to its floor. That's when the ocean rises. Sagara comes up out of the water in person, shining, garlanded, with the rivers around him, and speaks with folded hands. I can't change what I am. Earth, wind, sky, water, fire: each keeps its own nature, and mine is to be deep and hard to cross. I won't dry up. But if you build, I'll hold it up, and you already have the builder: Nala, son of Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods. Rama's arrow can't simply be put down, so he sends it north, and Valmiki says the land it struck became a desert. Now look at what just happened. The ocean is a god, with a voice and a nature of his own, and even Rama, Vishnu on earth, listens to him. Hindu tradition sees the whole world this way: earth, water, fire, air and space, the pancha bhuta, five elements, each with its own nature, each sacred. That's why Hindus bow to rivers, offer water to the rising sun, and call the earth Bhudevi, the goddess.
screen: `RAMA TAKES UP HIS BOW.` · `THE OCEAN RISES.` · `EACH KEEPS ITS OWN NATURE.` · `EVEN RAMA LISTENS.` · then, large: `THE FIVE ELEMENTS ARE SACRED.`

Try it now: rest a hand on the floor. If you pray, say it in your own words. If you don't, simply notice the ground holding you up, and thank it.

636.title: Nala's bridge
636.hook: five days, a whole army of builders, and the later stories that teach the power of Rama's name
636.carry: nama: Rama's name carries the stones
636.howItsDone: Many devotees practice likhita japa, writing Rama's name over and over in notebooks; pilgrims visit Rameswaram and Dhanushkodi, linked by tradition to the bridge, and the squirrel's story is a common children's tale.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, promised. The ocean rose as a god and said it couldn't change what it was, and your line was the elements are sacred, each with its nature.

Nala steps forward, and what he says is quietly funny. The ocean is right. I'm Vishvakarma's son, and I have my father's skill. I can build this. Then he adds, more or less: nobody asked me, so I didn't mention it. An army has been staring at an impossible sea, and the one person who could solve it was standing in the crowd, waiting to be asked. Then the work begins.
screen: `NALA STEPS FORWARD.` → `NOBODY ASKED ME.` → `THE WORK BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki loves the noise of it. The monkeys and bears pour into the forests and tear up trees by the thousand. They drag boulders down from the hills and heave them into the water with a sound like thunder. Some hold measuring lines while others lay the stones. And he counts the days: fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. In five days it's done, a hundred yojanas long, straight across the sea, and the army crosses to the shore of Lanka. Two beloved stories aren't in Valmiki. They come from later retellings and oral tradition. In one, a little squirrel rolls in the sand and shakes it onto the bridge, and Rama strokes its back; the stripes are his fingers. No offering is too small. In the other, Rama's name is written on the stones, and the stones float. That one carries a teaching Hindus take very seriously: nama, the divine name. In bhakti, God's name isn't just a label. Saying it, singing it, even writing it, is a way of being with God. The poet-saint Tulsidas goes further: he calls Rama's name greater than Rama himself, and many devotees read the floating stones that way: the name carries what hands can't. That's why many devotees fill whole notebooks with Sri Rama, written over and over, as a quiet prayer.
screen: `TREES, BOULDERS AND THUNDER.` · `FIVE DAYS, A HUNDRED YOJANAS.` · `THE SQUIRREL'S STRIPES.` · `STONES THAT FLOAT.` · then, large: `NAMA: THE NAME CARRIES.`

segments.voice: Many devotees practice likhita japa, written repetition: they write a name of God, Sri Rama, again and again, slowly, in a notebook kept just for that. Try a few lines now, on paper or in your mind. If you pray, write Rama, or the name of God that's yours, and let each one be a small stone on the bridge. If you don't, write one word that steadies you, slowly, and breathe between them.
The bridge. Setu. Built in five days by an army of monkeys and bears under Nala, a hundred yojanas long, carried by the ocean that promised to hold it up.

637.title: Vibhishana's crossing
637.hook: Ravana's own brother tells him the truth in council, is driven out, and comes to Rama for refuge
637.carry: sharanagati: I've come to Rama for refuge
637.howItsDone: Hindu tellers honor Vibhishana for his honest counsel in Ravana's hall, and Sri Vaishnava teachers hold up his coming to Rama as a model of sharanagati, taking refuge in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, built in five days under Nala, and your line, nama, Rama's name carries the stones.

Go back to Lanka, just after Hanuman left it burning. Ravana calls his council. A monkey has walked into his city, killed his soldiers and set his houses on fire, and an army is gathering across the sea. The ministers stand up one by one, and every one says the same thing. You've beaten the gods, king. Who is this Rama? We'll crush him. It's the sound of a room where everyone has learned what the boss likes to hear. Then one person stands up and says something else.
screen: `RAVANA'S COUNCIL.` → `EVERYONE SAYS THE SAME THING.` → `ONE VOICE SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: It's Vibhishana, Ravana's younger brother. Valmiki places this before the bridge is built; we told the bridge first, and now we step back. Vibhishana speaks carefully, like someone who loves the person he's about to anger. Give Sita back. Taking another man's wife was wrong, and it will destroy you, and all of us with you. Rama has done you no harm. Return her, and Lanka lives. Ravana won't hear it. In Valmiki his answer is cruel: better to live with an enemy, or a cobra, than with a kinsman who secretly works for your enemy. He calls his brother a disgrace to the family, and says anyone else who spoke like this would be dead already. So Vibhishana rises into the air with four companions and speaks from above the hall. You're my elder brother, and I owe you respect. I said this for your good. People who say pleasant things are easy to find. People who say hard, useful things, and people willing to hear them, are rare. Then he leaves. He crosses the sea, stops in the sky above Rama's camp, and calls down: I am Ravana's brother, Vibhishana. I've left everything behind. I've come to Rama for refuge. Hindus have a word for what he does: sharanagati, taking refuge, coming to God with nothing and asking to be held. Tradition remembers Vibhishana as a model of it. He doesn't bring an army or a bargain. He says who he is, says he's left everything, and asks. What Rama does with that, tomorrow.
screen: `GIVE SITA BACK.` · `A KINSMAN WORSE THAN A COBRA.` · `I SAID IT FOR YOUR GOOD.` · `I'VE COME FOR REFUGE.` · then, large: `SHARANAGATI: TAKING REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus have a short prayer of refuge they come back to. One is Sri Rama sharanam mama: Rama, you are my refuge. Sit quietly and bring to mind whatever you're carrying. If you pray, say it softly a few times, the way Vibhishana called down from the sky. If you don't pray, think of where you go when you need shelter, and let yourself arrive there for a few breaths.
